utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Lukic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Maslic. I've reorganised my questions a bit and I will not be introducing a number of documents, in order to expedite the procedure. We talked on Friday about this exchange in Dragalici about the reporting and the beating. I will be asking you about a number of details about this particular instance of exchange. But one particular question right now: If a person - I'm talking about a civilian person - is put on the exchange list and told to come in front of the bus from where they will depart for the exchange, can that person be prohibited from going to that exchange if that person is on the list?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any person which is on the final exchange list could go to be exchanged, and no one could take that person off the list or prevent that person from boarding the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the police -- could the police exercise any powers within its general competence to prohibit any person from boarding the bus?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the police never prevented anyone on the final list from boarding the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the police have powers to prohibit any person who was not on the list but wanted to get on the bus from boarding the bus?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could. No one who was not on the list could board the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could anyone except the police, apart from the police, also prevent the people from boarding buses, someone from among the members of the commission?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This particular instance of exchange which was held in Lipovac towards the end of January 1993, do you recall that particular instance of exchange, and what was characteristic about it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this exchange and its specific characteristics, its specific characteristics, were in the fact that this was members of the United Nations forces who undertook it upon them to carry out this entire exchange. It was the Russian battalion, as far as I could remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they actually do on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the United Nations forces -- rather, a soldier from among these troops took the lists from us, and they actually carried out the exchange. That was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone of you present when the people stated their desired options in front of the United Nations, or rather, Russian battalion troops? When you say "you," I mean your commission members and the other side.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, no one was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until which time were the premises of your social work centre and the local Red Cross chapter in the premises of the local community or the pensioners' centre, rather?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember the exact date, but it was sometime in 1993 that the -- we evacuated the premises of the Red Cross. And the centre was moved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it moved to? Tell us the specific location, if you can.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The centre was moved to the premises of what then was the public fund of pensioners or retired people and disability insurance of Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it is not in the building of Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were ever the offices of the Red Cross or of your centre in the actual building of Samac municipality, I'm talking about 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they never were in the building of Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any door in -- did any door ever in the building of Samac municipality bear the inscription of Red Cross organisation?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No room whatsoever ever bore the mark or the inscription of Red Cross in the municipality assembly building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please: What was actual characteristic of the work of your centre and of the Red Cross during 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the work of the local Red Cross and your centre at the beginning of the conflict, and you told us in general what it was about. But can you tell us whether there was anything specific in the work of the institutions in 1993, did they continue to work on the same subject-matter as in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was child welfare and protection issues, and the Red Cross -- the work done by this social work centre for child care and the Red Cross certainly in 1993 acquired a different dimension, as it were, namely, in the sense of the extent of their duties, the workload, so that their lines of work actually were brought into accord, evolved within the framework of what was prescribed under the law. What was specific was that day in and day out, the number of people in need of assistance kept growing, primarily because of the influx of a large number of refugees from the areas of -- the area of the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina and also Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Did the funds available to the centre increase also during that time or was it hard to get monies by that time? I mean the centre and the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The social work centre, as an institution, still did not have the financial means required, and we addressed the problems that we had to deal with exclusively on the basis of humanitarian assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the witness please be shown document internally marked PDB 144/3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who the author of this document is?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I wrote this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because there is no signature, so I wanted to clear this up.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is about what we did within the social work centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We shall not go into detail into the document. It is self-explanatory to the fullest, and the Trial Chamber will certainly be able to see that. Will you tell me: Who was it for? Who was it intended for? Who was it written for?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our standard practice -- it was the standard practice for the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly to be informed about the work of the service. So it was intended for the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections - and I believe that this has already been said at the beginning - can we be assigned an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D100/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We shall go back to the subject of exchanges. Tell me: From the moment when, in the fall of 1992, the commission was actually set up, and before that, and after that, when you started having direct contacts with the other sides, with their commissions, with the Croatian and Muslim sides, how often did you meet with them and how often did your commission -- all these commissions hold their meetings, and how often did you have to go outside Samac territory for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard to give you an answer in terms of a single figure, but I believe it was once a week that we held such meetings, went for such meetings with representatives of the commissions of the HVO, i.e., the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me: Do you know, from the beginning of 1993 and in the course, throughout that year, whether Miroslav Tadic did anything else apart from working on these exchanges?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which specific period, in 1993, from which period, from which time in 1993, but I believe that Tadic had no other assignments, no other duties, apart from this work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said at the beginning of your testimony that he worked for the civil defence. Can you actually define this period in 1993 when he no longer worked for them, or you noticed that he no longer worked for the civil defence? If you can just tell us the time more precisely, if you can.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was already in the first half of 1993 that he stopped doing work for the civil defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let us discuss a bit your work with the Muslim commission, or rather, the commission of the B and H Federation. So far we have more or less been talking about exchanges involving Lipovac and Dragalic, which is where the opposite side was the HVO or the Croats; right? How different was the form of negotiations with the Muslims and with the Croats? In what did the difference lie?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the security arrangements during meetings with these commissions differed; namely, there was less security when we had talks with the Muslim side, or rather, the security arrangements were more relaxed. And these meetings with the Muslim side were also less frequent. Both sides had their demands, their requests, for people to cross over to the other side, but there were much fewer people interested in actually crossing to the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explained this yesterday. You told us that the Muslims also wanted to go towards Croatia because that was the way to the west. Do you know what would have happened to able-bodied Muslims, what happened, actually, to able-bodied Muslims who went in the direction of the Federation during the exchange?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I heard from talking to these people, they actually avoided going to the Muslim side because, first of all, that would not enable them to go to a third country; and secondly, because they would be mobilised into units into which they didn't want to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the witness be shown document internally marked PDB 107/3. [In English] Put it on the ELMO, please. Put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just received information from the accused that they cannot see the ELMO on the monitors?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps we need assistance from the communications people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, you can put it in front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think all of us can see it. Anyway, we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Now it can be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, would you please take a look at this document. Is it familiar to you? My question is the following: Where did these persons report, and then what? When you'd compile a list like this, what would you do then?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These persons reported to the local Red Cross, and this list was used as a basis for showing to the Muslim side that these persons wish to cross over to their side, specifically, here to the municipality of Gradacac. All these persons had parts of their families in Gradacac, and that is why they had expressed their wish to go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These persons are from the municipality of Samac, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they expressed their wish to cross over to the other side for family reunification, because somebody had stayed behind in Gradacac: Wife, children, close family members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just spell this out precisely. Gradacac was a town that at that time was under the control of the army of the Muslim Federation, under the control of the Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like this document to receive a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D101/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this document -- how many pages does it have? The English translation which you have, how many pages does it have? Because it seems to be attached to another document which has -- can you please just lead us through so that we have the correct document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. I need to check this. No, no, no. It's only these persons on page 2. These five persons are also on the list. I mean, that is simply the order of the pages. I mean, from number 26 up to number 30 are the same persons, I mean those from 26 to 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only it's typed out a bit differently, but obviously the translation is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. This one that I have has up to 47 people. It has three sheets. The English translation, if you check. And it was signed by -- it shows as having been signed by the witness, actually. It continues from 31 to about 47. If your case is that it's only up to 30, fine. Just explain to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. My case manager just told me that one page was not attached properly, so it's simply this one page that is not attached properly in the copies that you have. But I have the right kind of document, so perhaps I can compare notes during the break with the registrar and then we'll see whether it's all right. I see that the registrar now has the right translation, the right kind of copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think part of the problem with what we have is that we have PDB 107/3, but then we have attached to it PDB 108/3 ter and 3, which is list of prisoners requested by the HVO Croatian Defence Council. So it seems as though we have attached to our English a separate document as well, in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously this is a mistake. We'll take care of it during the break. But perhaps now we can just have an ID number, if there's a problem, or perhaps we don't have to assign it a number one way or another and we can do it after the break. However, since we have provided a proper kind of copy to the registrar, perhaps we can go on. We don't have to deal with it straight away, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. We can go ahead with the number now that it has been explained. So the list is from 1 up to 47. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we shall have the number given by the registrar already.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we just have the number repeated from the registry, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I reconfirm that the number of the Exhibit is D101/3 [Realtime transcript read in error "D103/3"] and ter for the B/C/S version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just check with the registrar. I think that the number, the one that I established here, was D101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It's D101/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the transcript says D103. But I think we've clarified it now. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like another document to be shown to the witness. It is PDB 114/3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, this document is a bit illegible, but let me repeat what another witness in these proceedings said. It is extremely transparent. Would you give me your comment with regard to what you see over here? I am particularly interested in the second part of this document. Could you please explain that.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with this document. This is a list of persons who went for an exchange and who had expressed their wish to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were these persons brought to -- brought for an exchange to express their wish?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the representatives of the Muslim commission insisted on having these persons come because they did not believe that these persons did not want to cross over to the other side. And this was the usual practice, that the Red Cross and the commission would make it possible for each and every person to state their wishes and to see their family members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they state their views before members of the commission from both sides?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said already that usual practice was that they state their views before the Muslim commission and that they themselves agree with them, or rather, that they state their views before their commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question in relation to this subject: Were there situations when you asked for a Serb, a person who was on their territory, to come and to tell you personally that he didn't want to come to your territory?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The same kind of practice prevailed, and this list shows that there were persons who in the territory of the municipality of Gradacac and who did not want to come to our territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were such lists made often?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please assign a number to this document as well? I'd like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D102/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more document, the last one that I want to discuss with this witness, is the document that was internally marked PDB -- no. Sorry. I beg your pardon. This is a Prosecution document that was introduced by the Prosecution when they dealt with it at the end. It is P146/41. If you remember, it was Ms. Aisling who introduced this large number of documents, exchange lists, and they all got a joint number, that is to say, P146, and the particular list that I'm interested in is 41 [In English] It's a list from -- it's the last list, 29 of September, 1993. ERN -- excuse me. Let's see. No, not that one. The last one. This one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: What's the number? What's the number of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is P146/42.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me one thing: Lukavac, the municipality of Lukavac, was under whose control at that time?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality of Lukavac was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, the Federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what does this document show? Who are they addressing, and what is done with this document later, once it is handed over to someone?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a list where the representatives of the commission from the municipality of Lukavac address their requests to commissions of the municipality of Samac, the municipality of Modrica, and the municipality of Doboj, I think. But I think that most of the persons on this list are from Samac. So the requests pertain to those persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what do you do specifically when you get a list like this?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this kind of list, Red Cross employees would inform these families that somebody was looking for them and that they should state their wishes as to whether they want to cross over or whether they want to meet up at the separation line itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to move on to another matter related to the same subject. I have now prepared two brief video clips, about two minutes respectively, with this witness. I'm also -- I also have prepared the transcripts of these video clips. Now, why is this so important? These are two different exchanges, one with the Muslim side and the other with the HVO side. Each is actually half an hour. And the content of these video clips is the way it is, and I would like the Trial Chamber to be able to analyse these video cassettes later. I would now like to have this witness identify a few of the key persons involved. So we are going to be dealing with video footage of two minutes respectively from each tape, so it won't be any longer than that. Could the video director please play the first video clip? There is very little dialogue. This is the very beginning. This is the second paragraph on the first page. You can follow the dialogue. The dialogue that you will hear.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] I can hear you. Hello. Welcome. Can you hear us? We're already moving. Now you can do the same. Agreed. We are leaving now and see you at the same place. We are leaving. Mind those mines there. Bypass them. I have the feeling that this was done on purpose. Well, bon voyage. Did you see their police with white belts? Look at that. We haven't shaken hands. We don't know the exact results established by the International Red Cross commission, but we have representatives of the Red Cross here, and they will be in a better position to tell you. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that the original is barely discernible, if at all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] You should have called us. You should have told us that you would not be coming or that you would be coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, tell us: Where was this taken?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was taken at the separation line between the municipalities of Modrica and Gradacac. This is typical. This is how we met with the representatives of the other side. We see here the representatives of the local Red Cross of Modrica, Samac, Doboj, Brcko, and on the other side there are representatives -- members of the military commission from Banja Luka and from Bijeljina. And on the other hand, there are representatives of the military commissions from Gradacac, Tuzla, Gracanica, Lukavac, and activists of the Red Cross from those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Were there some mines on the road as you were going there? Did this happen often?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said a while ago that this way of contact was a high-risk one. But we did manage to reach agreements, or rather, the military commissions managed to reach agreements with unit commands. That is to say, during this period, while we were at the separation line, there should be a ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we play the video footage again from where we stopped it? Could we have it played on the monitor? Only from that point where we stopped, please. Could we see -- could we see that video footage again so that the witness could identify the persons there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me now: --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the man with grey hair, in uniform, on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the president of the military commission of the Tuzla district, Mr. Marko Duspara, representative of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he before the war, professionally speaking?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But as I spoke to him, I realised that he worked for the retirement insurance company in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the man next to him in uniform, a big man with black hair?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Mr. Milutin Grujicic, representative of the commission for exchanges of the 1st Krajina Corps from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have it played some more, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] These people did not report to me. Can we schedule this for Tuesday? I transmitted this, and Djoko was present there. Look, we are exposed to the danger of shelling. I apologise, Marko, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Faster, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] So we agreed that we would meet on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is this man, the man who is speaking?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Slobodan Despotovic from the municipality of Modrica. I believe he was a member of the military commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we continue showing the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is this man, the man with the glasses, the man who is sitting?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Matija Bodirogic, the man to the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. The man with the glass, wearing glasses, to the right, on the left side, this man in uniform, this -- no, no. I'm sorry. In the left bottom corner, sitting with the glasses.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, this is Matija Bodirogic, president of the military Exchange Commission from Bijeljina, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a good look. I'm not going to suggest anything to you, but is not this man from the Muslim commission?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I apologise. This is Mr. Safet Kikic from Gradacac, from the military commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what he did before the war?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He is a jurist by profession, a lawyer. He worked as a prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the technicians to play the second part of the video clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before they play that, I just want to be clear: The second part, it will be on the same video footage? Because I'm thinking about the numbering.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first footage running time is about 30 minutes and the second clip about 35. I just want while this is being rewound to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the fact that it was very hard for us to compile these transcripts because there are many people speaking at the same time. So that we really tried to do our best for every word to figure in the BH transcript. Perhaps there might be some unclarity in the translation into English, but I believe the transcript rather reflects the entire conversation rather well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So here we saw military personnel in uniform.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We can have this still here. It doesn't have to move. Do you know what this is, what this place is?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a meeting between representatives of the Croatian and Serbian sides. On the left, Croatian representatives Mr. Mijo Matanovic, Ante Kujic, and I do not know who the man in the centre is. And on the left side are representatives of the Serbian side, Mr. Grujicic, Mr. Simeunovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said to the left. You mean to the right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the representatives of the Serbian are on the right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we continue? Can the video director please play the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A little bit back, please. Stop here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is this man in a white shirt, on the left?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the left. This is Mr. Milutin Grujicic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is he in mufti?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this meeting was held in UNPA zone, the zone under the United Nations control, so one could not enter the zone in uniform, in military clothes, clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we be assigned a number for this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please. And the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To clarify my last question. It was page 19, line 4. I asked: Why was he wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video on the exchange of the civilians of Gradacac, 14th of May, 1993, will be assigned Exhibit D103/3. The English transcript of the video will be D103/3A and the B/C/S version will be D103/3 ter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now deal with the exchange which took place in December 1993, the end of December 1993. You mentioned that Hajra Drljacic was a neighbour of yours, a first-door neighbour of yours. Do you have any knowledge regarding her exchange? Did she address you? And I will simply ask you: Did you force her to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Mrs. Hajra Drljacic, a neighbour of mine -- this was an isolated person. She lived a rather lonely existence. She was not married. She did not -- she was not very -- on very good terms with the neighbours. She did not socialise much. She did have contact with me, and we were on good neighbourly terms, however. So she came to the Red Cross chapter often. She took the written messages from the International Red Cross there. And as far as I can remember, these messages were written to her by her daughter, who lived in Osijek. She often came to report, state her wish to be exchanged, and then she would change her mind and give up the idea. And I know that she asked me what she was to do, and I told her: This is your decision. You have to decide what it is that you want to do, and you have to tell your daughter so, so that she would know, and that she should not seek you if you don't want to go. So to her question what she was supposed to do, I told her that she should go to the line and state her views, state her preferred option there, and that she should also see her daughter. I don't know what she did, what she actually did, but I believe that she was later exchanged and went to live with her daughter in Osijek. I don't think that anybody else in the Red Cross told her anything else, because she was quite a sick woman, in quite poor health condition, and I'm sure that everyone would have helped her, given her condition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me whether, towards the end of 1993, any problems cropped up in the relationship between the Muslims and Croats in respect of the departures of Muslims into Croatian territory. Do you have any information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The representatives of the commission from Croatia, the Croats, told us that there were clashes between Muslims and Croats in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that such persons, such Muslim persons, would not be accepted, would not be admitted into Croatia. I didn't ask why. This is actually what I heard as having been stated in a statement by the president, the president of their commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how did this exchange actually proceed? Who went there? How was it carried out?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about the exchange of the 24th?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I mean the 24th of December, 1993, which is the last exchange.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negotiations were quite lengthy prior to that exchange, and so we said in the end, at this date, so that the exchange would take place before Christmas. So we agreed that it would take place on that date, at 1.00, in Dragalici. And as far as I can recall, there were Croats and Muslims in that exchange. And Serbs were also supposed to come from Orasje and Bukva Greda, the village of Bukva Greda in Orasje municipality, as well as Serbs from Orasje. However, we normally entered the UNPA zone. Members of the United Nations forces were there seeing that the standard procedure was being applied, as usual. So we entered the UNPA zone and we waited for the exchange to take place. It was standard practice for the troops always to be present on the spot. The representatives of the Croatian side failed to show up, so that a soldier of the United Nations went to inquire why, and we had no contact with them at that place. We couldn't have any contact with them there. The soldier was not given a reply and he just told us that there was no one on the other side. It was only towards evening that we were told that the representatives of the Croatian commission would come to deal with the problem. It was quite cold. People were unhappy, dissatisfied. But we could not return, go out of the UNPA zones because of the rules that we had to abide by, which were the rules applied by the senior -- by the battalion and the senior officer in charge, the commander of the Nepalese battalion told us that we couldn't leave the zone. So we waited. And in the evening, Mr. Marko Milos arrived in the area. He is a member, I believe, of the HVO military commission. And that was the first time when I saw him in uniform. He came and he apologised to the people in the bus, because it was indeed very hard to sit in the bus, where it was very cold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my correction of the transcript, page 22, line 2, the witness said that he could not return, go back from the UNPA zone.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On that occasion we asked Marko Milos why had all this been done in this way, and he said that he would have to apologise to the people, and he indeed apologised to the people. And he said that they were facing problems within their own leadership. I know that he then called his, as he said, boss, and that after a couple of hours that they came and that they promised that they would make it possible for the people to cross over where they wanted. To our question what about the Serbs from Orasje, that we had also agreed would be coming, he said that he was unable to bring them then because it was already late. It was already night. But that it was his desire for those citizens, for those persons, which included Muslims and Croats as well, to celebrate Christmas, but not in this way. So we accepted this proposal, and these people were then brought subsequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me just briefly whether before this exchange, Ivica Pandurevic came to see you, asking you for this exchange to be organised, without going into detail.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivica Pandurevic, as I've already said, was the commissioner of the Zasavica local community. He came to the Red Cross very often to deal with various humanitarian issues. But then, before that exchange, he came and told us that there were very many refugees in the village and that they were encountering problems with these people who had settled there from Zavidovici, Kakanj, Vares, and that they were having trouble with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have finished with all the exchanges. I will now proceed with the last set of my questions, within which I'm interested in a specific topic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any talk about money, any offers of money being made in connection with the exchanges, or any similar -- were any -- did you ever hear of anyone asking for money, demanding money? Was there any talk about such things?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard in town that there were such rumours, but I myself had no occasion to personally either witness or hear that somebody had taken money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to clear this matter up, to see -- to get to the bottom of such stories?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, once I got in touch with an officer in a brigade. I talked to him about this, and I told him that such practices needed to be punished very severely, if indeed there existed such practices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me whether you personally ever heard that Miroslav Tadic ever asked anyone for money or any kind of service.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard that Mr. Tadic asked anyone for money or any other services.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anyone give him money, even though he didn't ask for it, or anything else?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me now: You said at first that you knew Miroslav Tadic very casually before the war, but we had the opportunity of hearing that you met up often during the war. So we would like to hear your opinion about Miroslav Tadic as a person. What did you conclude about him after all those years that you worked together with him?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I knew Mr. Tadic only by sight from before the war. I met him during the war. I can say that he is a man who reacted very emotionally when it came to people and helping people. He made an effort to help them. He did not spare his own time, regardless of who this was about. He wanted to help, and I think that he did help whoever he really could have helped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any differences involved in terms of ethnic background, as relates to the persons he would help?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no difference, none whatsoever, regardless of ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, when you took part in the process of exchanges, what was your objective and what was your wish? What did you want to achieve through that kind of work?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I'm a social worker by profession, so I am a humanist. As I worked in the Red Cross, as a Red Cross activist, I had the opportunity and obligation to help people. And in contact with the representatives of the International Committee of the Red Cross and at their suggestions, and in view of their intention and wish to help people who were in trouble, in a war situation, they indeed did need help, within the local Red Cross, within the service for searching for persons, missing persons, it became necessary to make it possible for persons, that is to say, civilians, citizens, to express their wish to leave the territory of the municipality of Samac and reunite with their family members elsewhere. And within this effort and with that intention in mind, we had great support and assistance from the International Red Cross. We took part in this. And I think that we did carry out our mission, that is to say, helping people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was supposed to be my next question. Now, ten years later, after all of this happened, do you think that you accomplished your task? Did you achieve your objective, your wish, when you originally started doing this kind of work?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that we are looking at this with ten years' hindsight, and when we look at all the trouble that the citizens of the Samac municipality went through, I see that practically all these citizens have returned, and they live in their own houses in Samac. We live together as good neighbours. A very large number of these persons address both me and our activists with words of gratitude. They say that at the time they were in a situation that truly required help, and indeed they did get that help. Not a single citizen who is an ethnic Muslim or an ethnic Croat and who now lives here said anything bad to me. They said that they were not -- they never said that they were not satisfied with something. Of course, there wasn't enough food or medicine, but this kind of help that we did receive was equally distributed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have concluded the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Any other counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. Very well. Cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have some questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Cross-examined by Mr. Pantelic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Maslic. You just mentioned now a few examples of citizens of Samac who returned to Samac and who live there now. Do you know whether in mid-May, in 1992, in Budapest, in the presence of the International Red Cross, an agreement was signed among the warring parties in Bosnia? Because, after all, you did work for the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of such an agreement, but I'm not aware of any details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find out perhaps later that one of the important principles of that agreement was the return of civilians to their place of residence once the war is over? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, the witness has made his position clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: He heard of it, doesn't know any details. Details are now being sought. That can't be possible, as a mattered of logic. If he doesn't know any details, he doesn't know any details, and that's the end of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to clarify whether after or maybe a later stage of the war he has a personal knowledge about the principles of that quite important agreement, because he was chief of the local Red Cross. So let's find out whether he's aware or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: His answer is so categorical, that I'm not aware of any details, and that's it. So you can't start suggesting to him the details of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, Mr. Maslic: The presence of the International Red Cross, or rather, the representatives in Samac in 1992, you referred to these contacts, I mean, how would you describe this? Did they come every day, once every month, once every six months? How often were they present in Samac?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard to say now whether they were there every two or three days, whatever, but on average they came to Samac once a week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Were there any restrictions upon their movement in Samac? Was it possible for them to visit all the facilities they wished to see in Samac?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, every time they would come they would announce this to the police and they would say what they wanted to visit and where they wanted to go. As for contacts with the local Red Cross, they were geared exclusively towards humanitarian matters. That is what they were interested in and that is where we could render assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Maslic: Were there any protests by the representatives of the International Red Cross in 1992 and 1993 vis-a-vis the local organisation or some civilian authorities? Did they protest in any way?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for protests, there weren't any. I know that at that time Mr. Matteas, during a particular contact with us, said that he was satisfied with our efforts and that they should be kept up and grow from day to day so that we could attain our common objective: Helping people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that actually the ministry of the judiciary of Republika Srpska was in charge of exchanges, or rather, coordinating all of that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Blagoje Simic, in any way, affected the exchange process? Did he say who could be exchanged and who could not be exchanged? Did he behave in any discriminatory fashion towards the non-Serb population of Samac in 1992 and 1993? What is your personal knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the work I did, and the commission afterwards, I had no contacts whatsoever with Blagoje Simic in this regard. As far as I know, he did not participate in any way or did he show in any way that he wished to affect that part of our work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maslic. [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution has an application in relation to the -- before the cross-examination of this witness proceeds and I'd like to make the application in private session and in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. The witness will be led out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Di Fazio: MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown D146/ -- sorry. My apologies. P146/42.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You commented on this document earlier this morning. Who created this document?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was created by the Exchange Commission from Lukavac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which was in the control of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, forces of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's essentially a request on their part to you, and provides you with a list of people that they're interested in?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but not only to me, but also to representatives of other municipalities: Modrica, for instance, and Doboj also, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Dzemal Memic president of this commission also handling the exchange of prisoners of war, to and fro?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was on the civilian commission, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They've obviously taken pains, then, to distinguish between commissions that deal with the exchange and movement of civilians and POWs, haven't they? You look at the top of the document, it says it's a commission for the exchange and movement of civilians. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look under number 2. It refers to Latifa Jasarevic, daughter of Hamid, and claims that she is in Zasavica, in Bosanski Samac. Does that just mean that she was living there?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, she was not living there, but she was part of a group of citizens who had been taken to Zasavica from Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. The document is a little more explicit when it comes to dealing with number 9, Sabra Halilbasic, refers to Zasavica, Bosanski Samac, as a camp. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that it is written this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Plainly, then, the Muslim side was under the -- had the impression or took the view that Zasavica was a camp. Would you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of what is written, this was their opinion, but that was not the way it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Look under number 11, Meho Hurtic. It says that he's in Bosanski Samac in detention as a civilian. But that couldn't be, so could it, because you only held prisoners of war; no civilians were held in detention in Bosanski Samac, were they?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they could not be detained as civilians. But this is their information, on the basis of which this whole list was compiled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said, as far as I remember, that the detainees in Samac were detainees and not POWs. They were detainees because of some proceedings which were going on against them at that time. And when he did refer to POWs, it was in Batkovic, I believe. MR. DI FAZIO: I believe the thrust of his evidence was that they were detained and then taken to Batkovic. I'll provide the witness with an opportunity to clarify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were people kept in detention in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that these people had been detained, they were detainees. Why that was so, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you don't know why they were being detained in Bosanski Samac, that must have been one of the most compelling possible reasons for you to go into those places and to find out why they were being detained. Is that not so? You, who are concerned with humanitarian issues.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We certainly did deal with humanitarian issues, but we were unable to go into the reasons why that situation was the way it was. It wasn't allowed for us to do so as Red Cross activists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I take it, then, from your answer that you made efforts to gain access to the detention centres in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Red Cross activists of the local Red Cross chapter visited the detainees and rendered basic assistance to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As president of the commission, wasn't it incumbent on you to go along and have a first-hand view of the situation in the camps of the city, town, that you were responsible for?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went to these places myself, but the -- but other Red Cross activists did. As I mentioned, Mr. Vasovic, Mrs. Petkovic, and Mrs. Jovanovic, Anka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you take pains from them to find out why these people were being detained, what class of prisoner they might be? Because that was, after all, an extremely important thing for you to do, given your humanitarian brief.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly did take pains to find out in what kind of a situation these people were, what it was that they needed of relief, of assistance, whether they needed medical care, whether they needed food, and similar -- everything which is within the domain of the Red Cross's activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So therefore, you had a good, clear picture of what was going on in the detention centres, in the TO building, in the SUP, in the high school gym, in the primary school gym?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in respect of the Red Cross and the needs of these people that could be met by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's not my question. My question is very, very simple. As a result of your workers going into the detention centres, you formed a clear, good, solid view of conditions in those places I mentioned: In the TO, in the SUP, in the high school gym and the primary school gym?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that as this is on the basis of hearsay, this question would have to be based on what kind of information he got, whether this was sound information, and this is something that the witness has no way of knowing, because it is hearsay. So the wish and solid view is indeed not applicable in this particular case. It should be reformulated for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, especially when the witness has said that the other activists are the ones who actually went there physically. So maybe he got the information, but if you're asking for what conditions, be specific. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the activists who went into the detention centres in the TO building, in the SUP building, in the gyms in the primary school and the high school, did they provide you with the living conditions that the inmates were undergoing at the time?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The activists who went to these places told me that the conditions were poor, that there were people there in need of medical care, that there were people there in need of food, and that there were people there who wished to get in touch with their family members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you that there were people there who were being beaten, tortured, on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard them say that they had seen people with traces of beating, and this was conveyed -- this information was conveyed to the medical team who went there in order to extend protection to those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Dr. Brdar Ruza Masic one of the doctors who went to the detention centres?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that she was, but she did not go there alone. She was not the only one who went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, given that you had been informed of these humanitarian crises in this establishments, did you tell the Crisis Staff or report to the civilian authorities, the Executive Board, for instance, of what was going on in these detention centres?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not get in touch with the Crisis Staff, and as for the civilian authorities, that is, the Executive Board, I told them, and also to the police which was guarding these people, I told them about the situation which obtained there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the response of the police?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that this was no concern of the Red Cross, that these were people against whom there existed criminal charges, had been filed against them, and that we were to do our own work, which was the work of the Red Cross, and not the police's work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you take care to establish what sort of criminal charges had been laid against them? Did you find out?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no way I could find that out, nor had it been made possible for me, nor is that part of my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So therefore, you were faced with a situation where you had reported to you, from your own workers, evidence of beatings, evidence of poor living conditions in these places, and essentially, when confronted by police telling you it was none of your business, you accepted it. Is that the situation?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not accept it. I could not accept that. But as far as I remember, the representative of the Red Cross had a talk, a direct talk with the police about the situation and asked for certain measures to be undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just one small correction for the transcript. The witness was referring to ICRC, not the Red Cross, because so far when he said "Red Cross," he referred to the local Red Cross, and now he was referring to ICRC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That will be corrected. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you consider writing a report --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour, and my learned friend. Also another correction. It's page 44, line 21. Instead of "representative," I believe that we heard that it was president of Red Cross, local Red Cross, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Now that causes confusion. Maybe the question can be asked so that the witness can clear the identity of the persons. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the person from the Red Cross, and which Red Cross are you referring to, who had the direct talk with the police about the situation?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The representatives of the International Committee of the Red Cross. And in the first part, I said that we too, the local Red Cross, had informed the police about the situation in those places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the local Red Cross speak to the International Committee of the Red Cross regarding the conditions in the camps?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned Mr. Matteas Kind, the representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross, and I talked with him -- may I continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked with him about questions associated with these people who were detained. He told me that he himself would personally talk to and request from representatives of the police for these people to be protected, and also that the local Red Cross chapter would get adequately involved and help these people as much as possible within their terms of reference. I know that we were not informed by him about the results of these talks of his with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that we are missing something here in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the -- what we heard what witness said is that the representative, that gentleman with the name of Matteas, actually spoke with the detainees in the police station or TO. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you clarify that, Witness? What did you actually say?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Matteas talked with both the representatives of the police, every visit was announced, and he talked to them, but he also talked with the detainees, because, as he put it, he had been working on their records, on their registration, and every time he saw them he would take to them and from them written messages which were being communicated via the Red Cross. He would leave the empty forms with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But your position is that this man, Matteas, as a result of speaking to you, went to the police and confronted them about the conditions in the prisons?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This morning you were giving evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Di Fazio. Just in case you're moving on. I had one question following on from yours, for the witness. Mr. Maslic, under the terms of the United Nations Geneva Convention on the treatment of civilians in time of war of 1949, there are provisions which apply to delegations of the International Committee of the Red Cross, and one of the articles in particular, Article 143, does provide that the ICRC shall have access to all premises occupied by protected persons and shall be able to interview such persons without witnesses, personally, or through an interpreter. And I'm just wondering, given your conversations with the gentleman Mr. Matteas: Did he indicate to you how the detainees, the protected persons, in other words, that he spoke to, how they were selected? Did he pick the people he wanted to talk to or was he presented with certain people by the police? And the second part of my question is: Did he have the capability to interview such persons basically in private, without any members of the police being present? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, Mr. Matteas conducted all the interviews with the detainees. He was alone with an interpreter. He would not allow any other person to be present at such interviews, and the representatives of the local Red Cross never accompanied him there, because he would not let them. And he did invoke the convention. As for cooperation with the police and the presence of the police and the picking of the detainees with whom the interviews were to be conducted, I don't know about that. I don't know what kind of a relationship they had in that particular regard. But I do know that he always established such contacts after having announced his intention to the police, and he requested permission from them to go and visit these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know he was always alone with an interpreter and would not allow any other person to be present at these interviews? Were you there?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there. I was not with him. But during the talks, we always had -- and we always had talks in the local Red Cross after such visits, he always accentuated that he wanted and requested the authorities to enable him to do that, to conduct those interviews alone, himself. So I never was personally present there, and this is what he would say after these visits, coming to visit us in the Red Cross local chapter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he gave you to understand that, as a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross, he had no problems obtaining access to prisoners and speaking to them, and speaking to them in private? That's your position, that's what was reported to you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not claiming that he did not have any problems, but when visiting the local Red Cross chapter, he always emphasised the method and the procedure that he wished in terms of his gaining access to and having contact with the detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not suggesting that he was living an entirely problem-free life either. But essentially, he gave you to understand that, as the representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross, he was gaining access to all the prisoners he wanted to see, was being entitled to -- allowed to speak to them privately, and generally fulfil his role as a member of the International Committee of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is absolutely the same question to which the witness has replied. This is a repetition of the same question. The Prosecution wishes an answer to it again. MR. DI FAZIO: No. He said that the witness had -- wasn't claiming that the witness didn't have problems and that the witness emphasised the method and procedure that he wished to use in order to gain access. My question is a different thing, a different issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your position that this man, this had Mr. Matteas, essentially had no problem in gaining access to prisoners and being able to speak to them privately? Now, it's a question that can be answered with a simple yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Lukic's objection is that it's essentially the same question. Perhaps the part which doesn't appear to be similar with the previous question is that whether Mr. Matteas did fulfil his role as a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross, which is different from not having problems gaining access to the detainees and having interviewed, according to his own instructions. MR. DI FAZIO: That's, with respect, not exactly what I wanted. I just wanted this witness to make absolutely clear whether or not his position is Matteas could get access to the prisoners in an unhindered way and be allowed to speak to them privately. Now, that can surely be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but the witness did say -- he said that he -- he cannot say that Mr. Matteas did not have problems, but reported to him during their discussions that he asked the police for permission, he interviewed some detainees. MR. DI FAZIO: Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, earlier in your evidence you said that Matteas was able to confront the police regarding conditions in the detention centres. I take it that he would have wanted to do that in order to protest to them about the conditions that were in the -- that existed in the detention centres.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that he announced to the police that he would be coming and that he wished to discuss these persons and the conditions under which they lived. Now, whether he did intervene, and to what extent, is something that I don't know. I didn't have any information about that. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for one minute, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You agreed -- you agreed just moments ago that when he went to speak to the police, he confronted them about conditions in the prison. Your answer was yes. Now, that could only have been to protest about what the conditions were, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. This is just calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Oh, I see what you're talking about. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, this is the man who was there on the spot at the time, if Your Honours please, and who was observing Mr. Matteas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps it's the way you've put your question. If you can be specific. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The confrontation was a protest, was it not?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what form this took, this addressing the police, whether it was a protest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, one thing's for sure: He wasn't going to go to the police and compliment them or congratulate them on conditions in those detention centres, was he?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is inconceivable that Matteas was going to the police to compliment them or congratulate them on conditions in the detention centres?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. The witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that he went to the police station to congratulate them, but I do know that Matteas, through part of his work, that is to say, that which entailed contact with the local Red Cross, did express his interest in persons who were detained. As to what he talked about with the police, I don't know about that, but I know that he was interested in the conditions under which these people lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier this morning Mr. Lukic was asking you questions, and he asked you: "Tell me, Mr. Maslic: Were there any protests by the representatives of the International Red Cross in 1992 and 1993 vis-a-vis the local organisation, or some civilian authorities? Did they protest in any way?" And you answered: "As for protests, there weren't any. I know that at the time, Mr. Matteas, during a particular contact with us, said that he was satisfied with our efforts and that they should be kept up and grow from day to day so that we could obtain our common objectives: Helping people." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that you gave that evidence this morning, had it escaped your mind that Matteas had to go and speak to the police regarding the conditions in the TO building and the primary school gym and the high school gym?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He spoke about the conditions in general, and he asked for the Red Cross, the local Red Cross, to be included and to give help. The local Red Cross did what he asked for, that is to say, sent a medical team, sent a team of activists who went there and helped these people, helped them to the extent to which they could help them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I've heard your evidence on that, but that's not my question. My question is simple. This morning Mr. Lukic took you to this very topic and asked you about protests, and you said: "As for protests, there weren't any," that he was satisfied with your efforts. Now, you have agreed that Matteas was compelled to go and speak to the police regarding conditions in the prisons. Why didn't you mention that this morning when Mr. Lukic was asking you questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before the answer, lest the witness be confused: These were questions that were put by Mr. Pantelic, so in order to avoid any confusion on that score. MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly. I won't ascribe them to Mr. Lukic then. I'm quite happy for them to be ascribed to Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the question is: When Mr. Pantelic was asking you about protests, why didn't you mention this visit of Matteas to the police to complain about the detention centres?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not think that those were protests, that what Matteas said, because that's not what he addressed to the Red Cross. I said that he had been satisfied with his cooperation with us, and every time he insisted that it was necessary to make as many efforts as possible by the activists of the International Red Cross, and also we should go there more often and help these people. Now, whether he protested with the authorities is something that I don't know about. Generally speaking, when he spoke about the conditions in which the citizens of the municipality of Samac lived, he mentioned the persons who had been detained, and he spoke about their conditions too, and he asked for assistance to be given to them. He was satisfied with that assistance, and he did not lodge any protests as to the work of the local Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On Friday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In fact, I just have one question while you were pausing there, Mr. Di Fazio. Mr. Maslic, I wonder again whether Mr. Matteas ever spoke with you concerning, number one, whether he was able to pick the detention centre or camp that he wished to visit, again, according to that same Article 143 of the Geneva Convention, there is an obligation on the state concerned to allow the ICRC representatives to go to any camp or detention centre they wish. So I'd like to know whether Mr. Matteas ever told you that he had the freedom to pick the high school, the TO, wherever. And then secondly, number two, whether he had access to go wherever he liked in that particular building. Could he go to where the detainees slept? Could he visit the toilets and the wash areas, and so on? So could he choose the detention centre or camp? And secondly, did he have freedom of access to visit all of the rooms that he wished? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the persons who were detained were under police jurisdiction, and Mr. Matteas cooperated with the police in terms of announcing his visits, the visits themselves, the places he wished to visit.
